references.text: In the preceding verse ([ref:Joh 3:11|John 3:11]), Jesus says that "we testify to what we have seen", but Nicodemus and his like-minded peers do not accept the testimony. This forms the basis for the contrast in verse 12 between the earthly and the heavenly.
[ref:Joh 3:13|John 3:13] follows up directly and explains why Jesus is qualified to speak about heavenly things: no one has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man, who descended from heaven.

[ref:Joh 3:31-32|John 3:31–32] expands on the theme that the one who comes from heaven testifies to what he has seen and heard, yet no one accepts his testimony. Jesus is the only one who can speak about heavenly things with authority.

In [ref:Joh 6:61-62|John 6:61–62], Jesus uses a similar line of reasoning: if the disciples are offended by his current words, what will happen when they see the Son of Man ascend to where he was before? It is a parallel argument moving "from the lesser to the greater".

In [ref:1 Kor 2:13-14|1 Corinthians 2:13–14], Paul writes that the natural person does not accept what belongs to God's Spirit, for it is foolishness to him. This illuminates Jesus' point: whoever does not believe in the earthly things can even less grasp heavenly things.

[ref:Ordsp 30:3-4|Proverbs 30:3–4] asks the question: "Who has ascended into heaven and come down again?" The text emphasizes that knowledge of heavenly things is beyond human reach, which highlights Jesus' point that heavenly things are even harder to believe.

[ref:Jes 55:9|Isaiah 55:9] says that "as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways". This contrast between the heavenly and the earthly forms the background for Jesus' argument that whoever does not believe in the earthly things can much less believe in the heavenly.

[ref:Heb 8:5|Hebrews 8:5] speaks of how the earthly priests serve at a copy and shadow of the heavenly. The contrast between the earthly (the shadow) and the heavenly (the reality) illuminates Jesus' point that earthly things are easier to grasp than heavenly ones.

In [ref:Job 38:4|Job 38:4], God challenges Job with questions about the founding of the earth. The theme is related: humans barely understand earthly things – how then can they understand God's heavenly counsels?
